summary: From the Gangetic plain, Chandragupta I (c. 319–335) raised the Gupta dynasty to imperial rank; Samudragupta's conquests and Chandragupta II's defeat of the Western Satraps made it the dominant power of northern India, a 'Golden Age' of art and science. Skandagupta repelled the Huns c. 455, but after him the empire lost ground to feudatories and to the Alchon Huns under Toramana and Mihirakula, and it had faded by the mid-6th century.
details: In the early 4th century the Guptas were a minor dynasty in the Ganges plain: the founder Gupta and his son Ghatotkacha were called only 'Maharaja', great king. Chandragupta I took the grander title 'Maharajadhiraja', great king of kings, and issued gold coins. Many historians link his rise to his marriage with the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi, who appears beside him on those coins. His accession is often placed in 319–320, the start of the Gupta era, though who founded that era is uncertain. From its capital at Pataliputra the dynasty now began its rise to imperial power.

Chandragupta I's son Samudragupta took the throne around 335 and turned a regional kingdom into an empire. His courtier Harisena recorded his campaigns in a long inscription added to the Allahabad Pillar, an old pillar of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka. It says he 'uprooted' many kings of the north and annexed their lands, captured and then released kings of the south as far as Kanchipuram, and made frontier kingdoms pay tribute. At its height his direct rule stretched from the Ravi river in Punjab to the Brahmaputra in Assam, and he performed the Ashvamedha horse sacrifice to proclaim his imperial power.

Samudragupta's son Chandragupta II, also known as Vikramaditya, became emperor around 375; a later play claims he first had to remove an elder brother, Ramagupta, a story whose truth is disputed. He extended Gupta power by war and by marriage alliances, notably marrying his daughter Prabhavatigupta into the Vakataka dynasty of the Deccan. His reign is remembered as a high point of Gupta culture: the poet Kalidasa may have been his court poet, and the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Faxian, who spent about six years in the Gupta lands, described them as peaceful and prosperous. Under him the empire reached its height.

For more than two centuries the Western Satraps, Shaka (Indo-Scythian) rulers based at Ujjain, had held Gujarat and western Malwa, with ports such as Barygaza on the Arabian Sea. Chandragupta II campaigned in central India, and the Satraps' coins stop abruptly in the 390s, then reappear dated in the Gupta era, showing that he had conquered them. The exact date is unknown, somewhere between about 397 and 409. The victory carried Gupta rule to the western coast, and according to one theory Ujjain became a second Gupta capital under a royal prince, which may explain later legends of King Vikramaditya ruling there.

Chandragupta II's son Kumaragupta I ruled from about 415 to 455 and kept intact an empire reaching from Gujarat in the west to Bengal in the east. Little is known of his wars, but he performed the Ashvamedha horse sacrifice, a ritual claim to imperial sovereignty. He is usually identified with King Shakraditya, whom a seal found at the site and later Buddhist writers name as the founder of the monastery at Nalanda in Bihar, around 427. Nalanda grew into one of Asia's great centres of Buddhist learning, but late in his reign new enemies, perhaps the Pushyamitras or the Hunas, may already have threatened the empire.

Around 455 Skandagupta, son of Kumaragupta I, took the throne, possibly after a disputed succession. His Bhitari pillar inscription says he restored 'the fallen fortunes of his family', first against enemies usually read as the Pushyamitras and then in close conflict with the Hunas, probably the Kidarites, who had pushed into north-western India as far as the Indus. The date of the Huna war is uncertain, but his Junagadh inscription of about 457–458 already celebrates victory over foreigners. He kept the empire's inherited lands, though the cost of these wars drained its resources.

Skandagupta's last known date is about 467–468, and he is generally considered the last of the great Gupta emperors. He was probably followed by his half-brother Purugupta and then by a run of short reigns, including Kumaragupta II and Budhagupta. Gupta coins show that the dynasty lost control of much of western India after about 467–469. Former feudatories and provincial rulers grew more independent, and the empire, though still holding the Ganges heartland, was shrinking and weakening just as a new wave of Huna invaders gathered in the north-west.

The Alchon Huns, one of the Huna peoples from Central Asia, had established themselves in Gandhara and the Punjab. In the late 490s their king Toramana broke through the Gupta defences in the north-west, and much of the empire there was overrun by about 500. His inscriptions show him ruling Malwa and reaching northern Gujarat, and seals bearing his name and the title 'Huna king' found at Kausambi, on the Yamuna, suggest the city was sacked around 497–500, though one seal's authenticity is questioned. The Huns had torn away the empire's western provinces and now threatened its Ganges heartland.

Malwa in central India was a key Gupta province, and at Eran it was held by Bhanugupta, probably a local Gupta ruler or governor. An inscription at Eran, dated to Gupta year 191 (510 CE), records that he fought in 'a great battle' in which the noble Goparaja was killed and his wife burned herself on his funeral pyre, one of the earliest recorded cases of sati. The inscription does not say who the enemy was or who won. Many historians think Bhanugupta was defeated by Toramana and that Malwa passed to the Huns, although others read the battle as a Gupta victory.

Toramana's son Mihirakula extended Alchon Hun power across northern India and was remembered, especially by Buddhist writers, for destroying monasteries and killing monks. In 528 he was defeated by Yashodharman, an Aulikara king of Malwa ruling from Dashapura (Mandsaur), possibly together with the Gupta emperor Narasimhagupta. Yashodharman celebrated the victory on pillars at Sondani, near Mandsaur, boasting that even Mihirakula had bowed at his feet. The defeat ended the Alchon Hun era in India, but the winner was a new regional power rather than the Guptas, whose authority kept shrinking.

By the 540s the main Gupta line ruled only a reduced kingdom in the east, and Yashodharman of Malwa had occupied most of northern and central India around 532. The last known inscription of a Gupta emperor comes from the reign of Vishnugupta: the Damodarpur copper plate, which records a grant of land in the Kotivarsha district, at modern Bangarh in West Bengal, in 542 or 543. Royal land grants like this show where a king's authority was still recognised, so this one suggests that Gupta rule now survived mainly in the east, in Bengal.

Vishnugupta, reigning until about 550, is usually counted as the last recognised ruler of the main Gupta line, though the succession of the 6th-century Guptas is unclear. The empire had been worn down by the Huna invasions, by the rise of former feudatories and rivals such as Yashodharman of Malwa and the Vakatakas, and by the loss of trade and tax revenue. In the Ganges heartland its place was taken by the Maukhari and Pushyabhuti dynasties, who even copied Gupta-style silver coins. Northern India was once again divided among regional kingdoms.
